list.listitem: Glossitis may be due to a primary disorder of the papillae of the tongue or may be a feature of underlying conditions ranging from benign to malignant. C
Candida is the most common condition causing glossitis. C
Many irritants can be avoided to improve symptoms and resolve abnormal physical findings. Abnormalities that do not resolve should be biopsied. C

background.definition: Glossitis refers to inflammation of the tongue, often manifested by abnormalities of color, texture, or sensation.

list.listitem: No exact statistics are available for glossitis. Tongue lesions of any sort are found in 1.5% of children, 3% of adult nonsmokers, and 5% of adult smokers in mass screenings.
Diabetic patients have up to a 5% prevalence of glossitis in some populations.
The most common cause of glossitis is Candida infection.
Glossitis may be an important clue to underlying disease.
The most worrisome tongue lesions are white or red patches that could be malignant.
Irritants: smoking, alcohol, acid reflux, dentures, oral care product ingredients, spices, hot foods, flavorings such as citrus or peppermint.
Anemias: Iron deficiency, pernicious anemia, sickle cell anemia.
Other nutritional deficiencies: B2 [riboflavin], B6 [pyridoxine], B3 [niacin], B9 [folate], vitamin C, fat malabsorption; zinc malabsorption.
Trauma: burns, bites, injury.
Infection: Candida, herpes, Streptococcus, EBV [Hairy leukoplakia], CMV, syphilis, tuberculosis, COVID-19, and Whipple's disease.
Unknown: Geographic tongue, median rhomboid glossitis, erosive lichen planus, leukoplakia, oral malignancies, aphthous stomatitis.
Immune response: erythema multiforme, angioneurotic edema/allergic reactions, Behcet's syndrome, Sjogren's syndrome, Kawasaki disease.
Drug reaction: methotrexate, clarithromycin, trimethoprim, meropenem.
Other: amyloidosis, malignancy-associated Acanthosis nigricans.
The pathophysiology of glossitis is often due to atrophy or hypertrophy of the lingual papillae. Biopsies may reveal an inflammatory infiltrate depending on the etiology.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Poorly fitting dentures or oral appliances

list.listitem: Determine whether tongue is affected diffusely or in localized areas. Color changes and the presence of ulcerations or hypertrophic papillae are the key clues in narrowing the differential diagnosis. C
Refer for excisional biopsy promptly for leukoplakia, erythroplakia, or any suspicious or nonhealing lesions. Oral carcinoma may be invasive at the time of diagnosis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Common in streptococcal pharyngitis; feature of Kawasaki disease; also in oral allergy syndrome due to foods, accompanied by swelling and itching lips and throat

Differential.Differential_Name: Folate, niacin, B6, B12, or iron deficiency
Differential.Differential_Features: Presentation varies from erythema to pale atrophy

Differential.Differential_Name: Irritants, allergic reaction, or acid reflux
Differential.Differential_Features: Swelling and tenderness may be present
Often black, although nearly any color may be seen; disorder of desquamation usually from irritants such as tobacco, alcohol, medications

Differential.Differential_Name: Affects children, especially infants; 50% transmission to family members; papillae may have pseudopustular appearance

Differential.Differential_Features: One or several inflamed, tender fungiform papillae with red or white appearance; unknown cause, possibly minor trauma.
Malignancy-associated variety can cause hypertrophy of lateral tongue papillae
Pseudomembranous patches easily scrape off, hyperplastic patches do not

Differential.Differential_Name: Persistent plaque cannot be scraped off; idiopathic, premalignant; biopsy indicated
Thickened white areas on lateral surface of tongue commonly seen in AIDS patients; strong association with EBV
Irregular white areas may coexist with ulcerations, lacy reticular pattern seen on buccal mucosa

Differential.Differential_Features: May have ovoid plaques and/or ulcers

Differential.Differential_Name: Deficiencies of iron, B12, niacin, folate

Differential.Differential_Features: Ventral tongue, gingivae, labial, and buccal mucosal surfaces; see chapter on aphthous stomatitis
Usually multiple small ulcers but atypical presentation can manifest as cross-hatched fissuring diffusely
Blisters rupture to leave ulcers, may also see target lesions
Mouth rarely involved, diffuse blisters and ulcers
Mouth almost always involved, diffuse bullae rupture easily
Tip and lateral surfaces involved with erythematous, tender papules that ulcerate

list.listitem: The key element of the physical examination is to determine the color and texture of the tongue, eg, smooth or rough, pale or reddened; and whether the process is diffuse or patchy. A gauze square is extremely useful to grasp and manipulate the tongue. Evaluate all tongue surfaces, including ventral and lateral posterior areas.
Altered taste sensation or glossodynia may cause difficulty with eating.
Weakness or other anemia symptoms may be present in deficiency syndromes. Ask about dietary avoidances that cause nutritional deficiencies, especially iron or B vitamins.
Also elicit any history of diabetes, malabsorption syndromes, HIV disease, autoimmune or rheumatologic diseases, and their associated symptoms.
Determine tobacco or alcohol use, oral hygiene habits, medications.
Examine skin for clues to systemic diseases. Uveitis and genital ulcers may be present in Behcet's syndrome.
Fever is present in 40% of patients with eruptive lingual papillitis.

If white patches are seen, the most important step is to do a scraping with a tongue blade to evaluate for thrush. Lesions scrape off with difficulty, leaving a tender red base that may bleed easily. Do a KOH stain to look for characteristic hyphae, or a Gram stain to reveal the yeast.
If immunodeficiency is suspected, consider serum glucose testing to diagnose diabetes and HIV testing for AIDS.

If the tongue is smooth, the most common cause is an anemia, so perform a CBC, serum iron and ferritin to look for iron deficiency anemia, and serum B12 and RBC folate to diagnose the macrocytic anemias.
A red, irritated tongue may be due to gastroesophageal reflux disease. Helicobacter pylori testing and radiologic or endoscopic evaluation should be considered.
A solitary, atypical red patch that is not typical for median rhomboid glossitis, ie, erythroplakia, has a very high likelihood of dysplastic or malignant changes and must be biopsied.
A rapid streptococcal screen is helpful in determining whether a "strawberry tongue" is due to streptococcal pharyngitis.
For any unusual or perplexing lesion, perform a biopsy. This is mandatory for a suspicious white or red patch or for any nonhealing lesion.
If the initial workup fails to yield clues, consider unusual etiologies; check a VDRL for detecting syphilis and a PPD for tuberculosis.
Examine the tongue for color changes, and whether a diffuse, homogenous process is evident versus changes that are patchy or localized.
Look for ulceration or diffuse atrophy or hypertrophy. See Differential Diagnosis for grouping of findings.

Candida is the most common diagnosis, often due to underlying immunosuppression such as in diabetes, AIDS, cancer, or the increased susceptibility of infancy; use of antibiotics, steroids, or cancer chemotherapy; xerostomia resulting from autoimmune diseases or radiation therapy; or smoking.

Acid reflux and anemias are the most common conditions causing diffuse glossitis. Empiric therapies for these conditions can be considered early in the course of treatment, or when other therapies fail to improve findings or symptoms.
Biopsy is recommended for any suspicious lesions.
Treat pain and irritation symptoms with topical anesthetics and soothing mouth rinses. C
Treat Candida with antifungal therapy. B
Supplement deficiencies of iron and B vitamins. C
Treat underlying systemic conditions to improve glossitis as a symptom. C

To decrease glossodynia, use over-the-counter topical anesthetic agents such as 2% lidocaine viscous solutions to "swish and spit." Other soothing mouth rinses include sodium bicarbonate solutions, carbamide peroxide 10% drops, or a mixture of kaolin-pectin and diphenhydramine to coat painful ulcerated lesions.
Topiramate and gabapentin have been proposed for treatment of idiopathic glossodynia.
Candida is treated with oral fluconazole or topical antifungals such as nystatin oral suspension.
Supplement iron and vitamin deficiencies. Empiric supplementation is often tried when malnutrition exists, when other modalities fail, or when symptoms persist without an obvious cause.
Symptomatic lichen planus is treated with a topical steroid preparation such as clobetasol propionate as an ointment or tacrolimus powder in Orabase 0.1% 3 times daily for 2 weeks.
Tetracycline oral rinses may be tried for the painful ulcers of inflammatory conditions such as Behcet's syndrome.
Treat acid reflux with H2-blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and regimens for H. pylori if indicated.
Artificial saliva is useful in Sjogren's syndrome.
Appropriate systemic therapy for streptococcal infections, Kawasaki syndrome, pemphigus, bullous pemphigoid, syphilis, and tuberculosis.
Suspicious lesions, erythroplakia, and leukoplakia are best treated with surgical excision for microscopic examination.
Reassurance for benign conditions, when asymptomatic, such as median rhomboid glossitis.
Avoid smoking and smokeless tobacco to reduce irritation. This is key in improving the coloring and severity of (black) hairy tongue.
Other substances, which can cause or aggravate glossitis and glossodynia, include hot, spicy, or acidic foods and beverages, whitening toothpastes, harsh mouthwashes.
Tongue brushing and scraping are useful for hygiene in hairy tongue.
Glossitis can be improved by treating underlying immunodeficiencies, eg, optimizing glucose control in diabetes and using appropriate medication to improve CD4 cell counts in AIDS.
Rinse mouth after use of inhaled steroids to decrease risk of Candida.
Refer to a dentist for poorly fitting dentures or oral appliances when traumatic irritation is problematic.
Refer to a dental hygienist to instruct in proper mouth and tongue care.
Refer to an oral surgeon or ENT specialist when malignancy is suspected or diagnosed; diagnostic excision is the treatment of choice for leukoplakia, erythroplakia, or any nonhealing lesion.
Prognosis varies and depends on underlying condition/cause. C
Candida responds well to drug therapy, normalization of hyperglycemia, and decreased steroid use. B
Persistent white or nonhealing lesions may have ominous prognosis if malignant. A
